shape.subject: Mathematics
shape.scope: Numbers and their operations (primes, HCF/LCM, squares/cubes/roots, standard form, estimation, significant figures); ratio and proportion (incl. map scales, direct and inverse proportion); percentage (incl. reverse percentage); rate and speed (incl. average speed, conversion of units); financial mathematics (simple and compound interest, hire purchase, money exchange, taxation, utilities bills); algebraic expressions and formulae (expansion, factorisation incl. grouping and quadratic trinomials, algebraic fractions, changing the subject, algebraic identities); functions and graphs (linear, quadratic incl. completed-square and factorised forms, cubic, reciprocal y=a/x and a/x^2, exponential y=ka^x, drawing on a grid from a table of values, gradient of a curve by a tangent, solving equations by drawing a suitable line); equations and inequalities (linear, simultaneous linear, quadratic by factorisation / completing the square / the formula, fractional equations reducing to quadratics, linear inequalities incl. double inequalities, word problems leading to these); set language and notation (union, intersection, complement, subsets, Venn diagrams with numbers of elements); matrices (display of information, addition, scalar multiplication, multiplication of two matrices, interpretation of the product; no inverses); problems in real-world contexts (reading tables and information sheets, making and justifying a decision, estimating a cost or a quantity); angles, triangles and polygons (angle properties of parallel lines, triangles, quadrilaterals and regular polygons; construction with ruler, compasses and protractor: perpendicular bisectors and angle bisectors; scale drawings); congruence and similarity (tests, ratios of lengths, areas and volumes of similar figures and solids); properties of circles (symmetry properties: equal chords, perpendicular from centre, tangents from a point; angle properties: angle at centre, angle in a semicircle, angles in the same segment, opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral, tangent-radius; reasons stated); Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry (sine, cosine and tangent for acute and obtuse angles, sine and cosine rules, area of a triangle as ½ab sin C, bearings, angles of elevation and depression, simple 3-D problems); mensuration (area of a triangle, parallelogram, trapezium, circle; arc length and sector area with the angle in RADIANS or degrees; surface area and volume of a prism, cylinder, pyramid, cone and sphere; composite solids); coordinate geometry (gradient, length, midpoint is NOT required, equation of a straight line y=mx+c, parallel lines, area of a rectilinear figure by shoelace is NOT required — use base×height or split into triangles); vectors in two dimensions (column vectors, magnitude, position vectors, addition, scalar multiples, collinearity, expressing one vector in terms of others, ratios of areas of triangles with a common height or on the same base); data handling and analysis (tables, bar charts, pie charts, pictograms, line graphs, histograms with equal class widths, dot diagrams, stem-and-leaf, box-and-whisker plots, cumulative frequency curves, median, quartiles, percentiles, range, interquartile range, mean and standard deviation for grouped and ungrouped data, comparing two distributions in context); probability (single events, combined events by possibility diagrams and tree diagrams, with and without replacement, mutually exclusive and independent events). NOT in 4052: calculus, logarithms, surds, the binomial theorem, trigonometric identities, the R-formula, quadratic inequalities, matrices inverses and determinants, vectors in three dimensions, the shoelace formula, the midpoint formula.
shape.register:
REGISTER — how SEAB asks (4052)
- Plain, exact, economical English. Instructions are imperatives: Find, Calculate, Work out, Write down, Simplify, Factorise, Expand, Solve, Show that, Explain why, Give a reason, Complete the table, Draw, Describe, Estimate, Express, State.
- Parts are labelled (a), (b), (c), with sub-parts (i), (ii). Every part carries its marks. A 1–3 mark question is often a single unlabelled part.
- A scientific calculator is allowed on BOTH papers. Never write "a calculator must not be used". The paper's rubric already says: non-exact answers to 3 significant figures, angles to 1 decimal place, π = calculator value or 3.142 — so a question states a precision only when it wants something else ("correct to 2 decimal places", "in its simplest form", "in terms of π", "as a fraction in its lowest terms", "in standard form", "to the nearest cent").
- Angles are in DEGREES with the degree sign ($58^\circ$); a sector angle in radians is stated as "1.8 radians". Bearings are three-figure ($048^\circ$). Money is dollars and cents ($\$92.75$).
- Contexts are short, concrete and Singaporean-neutral (a garden fountain, a box of apples, a map of Singapore, a candle business): the situation in one or two sentences, units given, then the parts. Never chatty, never a story.
- "Show that" states its target exactly ("Show that $x^2 - 102x + 1440 = 0$", "Show that $p = 2.5$") and a later part uses it. "Explain why …" / "Give a reason for your answer" / "Is he correct?" parts are worth 1 mark and expect one sentence with a number in it. A circle-properties question says "Give a reason for each step of your working."
- Statistics and probability parts ask for interpretation in context ("By commenting on the means and the standard deviations, compare …", "Explain what this tells you about …").
- Paper 1 (27 short questions, 90 marks): each question tests ONE idea in 1–7 marks, answered in the space provided; the paper walks the syllabus (number, algebra, geometry, statistics interleaved), with the vector and mensuration questions near the end.
- Paper 2 (9 long questions, 90 marks): each question is 8–12 marks in 3–5 parts. Early questions are ALGEBRA MEDLEYS whose parts (a), (b), (c), (d) are separate short problems on different algebra skills. Later ones are one context developed through parts: a graph question (a table of values with two blanks, "On the grid, draw the graph of …", a gradient by a tangent, "By drawing a suitable straight line, solve …"), a trigonometry-on-the-ground question with bearings and a mast, a statistics + probability question over a table or histogram, a circle-properties + circular-measure question, a speed/quadratic question ("Show that … = 0", solve to 2 decimal places, reject a root, interpret), and the last question is a PROBLEM IN A REAL-WORLD CONTEXT: an information sheet (a table of prices, rates or measurements) followed by parts that end in a 5–7 mark "Suggest a suitable … Justify your answer" or "Is it worth …? Show your working" decision.
- Marks follow the work: about 1 mark per 1.5 minutes. 1 mark: read/state/one-line. 2 marks: one routine. 3–4 marks: a short chain. 5–7 marks: a multi-step argument or a decision with working.

title: E Math · Set 2 · Paper 2 · O-Level format

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
$T = \sqrt{\dfrac{2p + 5}{p - 3}}$
Rearrange the formula to make $p$ the subject.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
Find the greatest possible value of $\dfrac{7}{x^2 - 3x + 4}$.
Show your working.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Use algebra to explain why the sum of the squares of any three consecutive integers is never a multiple of 3.
parts.answer: With the integers $n - 1$, $n$, $n + 1$, the sum of their squares is $3n^2 + 2$, which is 2 more than the multiple of 3, $3n^2$, so it leaves remainder 2 when divided by 3 and is never a multiple of 3.

question.answer: (a) $2 \times 3^{n}$; (b) $p = \dfrac{3T^2 + 5}{T^2 - 2}$; (c) $4$; (d) $(n-1)^2 + n^2 + (n+1)^2 = 3n^2 + 2$, which is 2 more than a multiple of 3, so never a multiple of 3.
skills: rewriting $9^{n}$ as $3^{2n}$ and taking out the common power factors $3^{2n}$ above and $3^{n}$ below to simplify a quotient of a sum and a difference of powers with a variable index to an expression in $n$
making a subject that appears in both the numerator and the denominator of a fraction under a square root
finding the greatest value of a fraction whose denominator is a quadratic with no real roots, by completing the square to find the least value of the positive denominator
proving by expansion, with the unknown introduced by the candidate, that the sum of the squares of three consecutive integers is always 2 more than a multiple of 3
question.solution:
(a) Write every power with base 3: $9^{n} = (3^{2})^{n} = 3^{2n}$, and $3^{2n+1} = 3 \times 3^{2n}$.
Numerator: $3^{2n+1} + 9^{n} = 3 \times 3^{2n} + 3^{2n} = 3^{2n}(3 + 1) = 4 \times 3^{2n}$
Denominator: $3^{n+1} - 3^{n} = 3 \times 3^{n} - 3^{n} = 3^{n}(3 - 1) = 2 \times 3^{n}$ [M1 for a correct common factor taken out of the numerator or of the denominator]
$\dfrac{3^{2n+1} + 9^{n}}{3^{n+1} - 3^{n}} = \dfrac{4 \times 3^{2n}}{2 \times 3^{n}} = 2 \times 3^{2n - n} = 2 \times 3^{n}$ [A1 for $2 \times 3^{n}$ or $2(3^{n})$]
(Check: $n = 1$ gives $\dfrac{27 + 9}{9 - 3} = \dfrac{36}{6} = 6 = 2 \times 3^{1}$; $n = 2$ gives $\dfrac{243 + 81}{27 - 9} = \dfrac{324}{18} = 18 = 2 \times 3^{2}$.)
Common errors: dividing the indices instead of subtracting them, $\dfrac{3^{2n}}{3^{n}} = 3^{2}$, which gives $18$; cancelling terms rather than factors, $\dfrac{3^{2n+1}}{3^{n+1}} + \dfrac{9^{n}}{-3^{n}} = 3^{n} - 3^{n}$, which gives $0$; adding the indices of a sum, $3^{2n+1} + 3^{2n} = 3^{4n+1}$. Substituting a value of $n$ gives only a number (6 when $n = 1$), not the simplified expression, and earns no marks.

(b) Square both sides: $T^2 = \dfrac{2p + 5}{p - 3}$ [M1]
$T^2(p - 3) = 2p + 5$
$pT^2 - 3T^2 = 2p + 5$
Collect the terms in $p$ on one side: $pT^2 - 2p = 3T^2 + 5$ [M1]
$p(T^2 - 2) = 3T^2 + 5$
$p = \dfrac{3T^2 + 5}{T^2 - 2}$ [A1]
(Check: $T = 3$ gives $p = \dfrac{32}{7}$, and $\dfrac{2p + 5}{p - 3} = \dfrac{99/7}{11/7} = 9 = 3^2$.)

(c) Complete the square for the denominator:
$x^2 - 3x + 4 = \left(x - \dfrac{3}{2}\right)^2 - \dfrac{9}{4} + 4 = \left(x - \dfrac{3}{2}\right)^2 + \dfrac{7}{4}$ [M1]
Since $\left(x - \dfrac{3}{2}\right)^2 \ge 0$ for all $x$, the denominator is always positive and its least value is $\dfrac{7}{4}$, when $x = \dfrac{3}{2}$. [M1]
The numerator 7 is fixed and the denominator is always positive, so the fraction is greatest when the denominator is least.
Greatest value $= 7 \div \dfrac{7}{4} = 4$ [A1] (when $x = 1.5$)
Common error: substituting $x = 0$ to get $\dfrac{7}{4}$.

(d) Let the three consecutive integers be $n - 1$, $n$ and $n + 1$, where $n$ is an integer. [B1]
Sum of their squares $= (n - 1)^2 + n^2 + (n + 1)^2$
$= n^2 - 2n + 1 + n^2 + n^2 + 2n + 1$
$= 3n^2 + 2$ [M1]
$3n^2$ is a multiple of 3, so $3n^2 + 2$ is 2 more than a multiple of 3: it leaves a remainder of 2 when divided by 3.
So the sum of the squares of any three consecutive integers is never a multiple of 3. [A1]
(Alternative: with $n$, $n + 1$, $n + 2$ the sum is $3n^2 + 6n + 5 = 3(n^2 + 2n + 1) + 2$, the same conclusion.)
Checking numerical examples only (for example $1^2 + 2^2 + 3^2 = 14$) is not an explanation and earns no marks.
question.syllabus_check: All four parts are inside 4052 and use no A-Math technique. (a) laws of indices with a variable index: a power of a power ($9^{n} = 3^{2n}$), $3^{2n+1} = 3 \times 3^{2n}$ and the division law $3^{2n} \div 3^{n} = 3^{n}$, with a common factor taken out of a sum and a difference of powers (Numbers and algebra: indices). (b) changing the subject of a formula in which the subject appears twice and the formula involves a square root and an algebraic fraction (Algebraic expressions and formulae). (c) a quadratic expression written in completed-square form to find its least value (Functions and graphs: quadratic functions in completed-square form); the argument uses only that a square is never negative, not a quadratic inequality, and no calculus. (d) expansion of squared brackets used to prove a property of integers (Algebraic expressions: expansion). No partial fractions, no surds, no simultaneous non-linear equations, no combining of fractions and no fractional equation.
question.originality_note: Written as an algebra medley whose parts are all different skills from the earlier Sets. No part combines algebraic fractions or solves a fractional equation (Set 1 P2 Q1(c),(d), Set 2 P1 Q5, Set 1 P1 Q11). (a) is not GCE 2025 P2 Q5(a) (a sum of two equal numeric powers giving a single power of 2): here the index is a variable, a power of 9 must first be rewritten as a power of 3, different common powers are taken out above and below, and the fraction simplifies to an expression in $n$ that no substitution can give; it is also unlike the common-base index equations of Set 1 P2 Q4(b) and Set 1 P1 Q16. (b) differs from Set 1 P1 Q12(b) (expand and cancel the $x^2$ terms) and from GCE 2023 P2 Q2(c)(ii) by the square root over a fraction with the subject in both numerator and denominator. (c) finds the maximum of a reciprocal from the minimum of a quadratic with no real roots; Set 2 P1 Q6 found the maximum of a parabola from its roots. (d) is a divisibility-by-3 proof by expansion with the candidate choosing the variable; Set 1 P1 Q25(b) argued the parity of a given $n^2 + n + 1$, and GCE 2024 P1 Q23(a) the parity of a given $y$.

answers.(d): shown: (n-1)^2 + n^2 + (n+1)^2 = 3n^2 + 2, which leaves remainder 2 when divided by 3, so it is never a multiple of 3

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both 5/3. Checked: numerator 3^{n-1}(9+1), denominator 3^{n-1}(9-3), ratio 10/6 = 5/3 for every n (verified n = 1..5).

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Both p = (3T^2 + 5)/(T^2 - 2). Checked symbolically: square, multiply out, collect the p terms, factorise.

verdict.key_verdict: The setter and the blind examiner agree on every part, and I checked each part independently: the key is right.
fixes: (a) has a shortcut. 'Find the exact value' tells the candidate that the answer does not depend on n, so putting n = 1 gives (9 + 1)/(9 - 3) = 5/3 in one line. The setter's own check line does exactly this, and it skips the factorising the part exists to test. Set 1 P2 Q1 has no part that can be beaten this way. Do not turn (a) into a 'show that it is independent of n', because (d) is already the proof.

Split the setter's skills array into four entries, one per part. At present the second entry joins (b) and (c) with a semicolon. Replace the topic tag 'Algebra (Fractions)': no algebraic fraction is combined or simplified. Use 'Algebra (Quadratic Graphs)' for the completing-the-square extreme value in (c).
Register, a light edit: in (b), write 'Rearrange the formula to make $p$ the subject.' (SEAB's wording, GCE 2023 P2 Q2(c)(ii)).
verdict.why: This is a P2 Q1 algebra medley of the 2024/25 kind (GCE 2025 P2 Q1 [2,2,3,3]). Each part has a twist. The candidate makes the decisions in (c), which is unscaffolded (complete the square, then take the reciprocal of the least value), and in (d), where the candidate chooses the three integers and proves the result: these two parts carry 6 of the 11 marks. The numbers are clean and the traps give tidy wrong answers (-1/3 from cancelling, 7/4 from x = 0). It is as demanding as Set 1 P2 Q1 and uses different skills (not fractions or fractional equations; different from Set 1 P1 Q25(b) and Set 2 P1 Q6). Only (a) needs a light edit, because substituting n = 1 bypasses its idea.

question.stem:
A factory has two machines, $P$ and $Q$, for making paper bags. Each order is for the same number of paper bags. Each machine works at its own constant rate.
Working on its own, machine $P$ takes $x$ hours to complete an order.
Working on its own, machine $Q$ takes 2 hours less than machine $P$ to complete an order.
On Monday, both machines start work on an order at 8.00 a.m. Machine $P$ breaks down at 9.20 a.m. Machine $Q$ continues on its own and completes the order at 12.30 p.m.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Show that $6x^2 - 47x + 16 = 0$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
By solving the equation $6x^2 - 47x + 16 = 0$, find the time that machine $Q$ takes to complete an order on its own.
Give your answer in hours and minutes, correct to the nearest minute.
parts.answer: 5 hours 29 minutes ($x = 7.48$; $x = 0.36$ rejected because $x - 2$ would be negative)

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
On Tuesday, machine $P$ has been repaired. Machine $Q$ starts work on another order on its own at 8.00 a.m. Machine $P$ starts work on the same order later that morning, and the two machines then work together until the order is completed at 12 noon.
Find the time at which machine $P$ starts work.
Give your answer correct to the nearest minute.

skills: work-rate model: each machine's share of an order as working time times its rate, with the working times read from clock times (1 h 20 min and 4 h 30 min, the faster machine working through the breakdown), summed to one whole order and cleared to a quadratic
choosing the valid root when both roots of the quadratic are positive (the other machine's time x - 2 must be positive), then giving the other machine's time in hours and minutes

reversed work-rate: machine P's working time found from the share of the order left after machine Q's 4 hours of work (Q works throughout, first alone, then with P), counted back from 12 noon to a start time
question.solution:
(a) Machine $P$ works from 8.00 a.m. to 9.20 a.m., which is 1 h 20 min $= \frac{4}{3}$ h.
Machine $Q$ works from 8.00 a.m. to 12.30 p.m. (it does not stop when $P$ breaks down), which is 4 h 30 min $= \frac{9}{2}$ h.
In 1 hour, $P$ completes $\frac{1}{x}$ of an order and $Q$ completes $\frac{1}{x - 2}$ of an order.
Fraction of the order done by $P$ $= \frac{4}{3} \times \frac{1}{x} = \frac{4}{3x}$; fraction done by $Q$ $= \frac{9}{2} \times \frac{1}{x - 2} = \frac{9}{2(x - 2)}$.
Together they complete one whole order: $\frac{4}{3x} + \frac{9}{2(x - 2)} = 1$.
Multiply both sides by $6x(x - 2)$: $8(x - 2) + 27x = 6x(x - 2)$
$8x - 16 + 27x = 6x^2 - 12x$
$35x - 16 = 6x^2 - 12x$
$6x^2 - 47x + 16 = 0$ (shown)
[B1 both working times in hours, M1 rates $\frac{1}{x}$ and $\frac{1}{x-2}$, M1 fractions summed to 1, M1 clearing the denominators, A1 given equation with no error]
(b) $x = \frac{47 \pm \sqrt{(-47)^2 - 4(6)(16)}}{2(6)} = \frac{47 \pm \sqrt{1825}}{12}$
$x = 7.4767$ or $x = 0.35667$ (7.48 or 0.36 to 2 decimal places)
$x = 0.357$ is rejected: machine $Q$ would take $x - 2 = -1.64$ hours, which is impossible (also, $P$ could not work for 1 h 20 min on an order it finishes on its own in about 21 minutes).
Time for $Q$ on its own $= 7.4767 - 2 = 5.4767$ h.
$0.4767 \times 60 = 28.6$ min, so the time is 5 hours 29 minutes (to the nearest minute).
[M1 correct substitution into the formula, A1 $x = 7.48$ with the other root rejected, A1 5 h 29 min]
(c) Machine $Q$ works from 8.00 a.m. to 12 noon, which is 4 h.
Fraction of the order done by $Q$ $= \frac{4}{5.4767} = 0.73037$.
Fraction left for $P$ $= 1 - 0.73037 = 0.26963$.
$P$ completes $\frac{1}{7.4767}$ of an order per hour, so the time $P$ works $= 0.26963 \times 7.4767 = 2.0159$ h.
$0.0159 \times 60 = 0.96$ min, so $P$ works for 2 h 1 min (to the nearest minute).
$P$ starts at 12 noon $-$ 2 h 1 min $=$ 9.59 a.m.
(Using $x = 7.48$: $\frac{4}{5.48} = 0.72993$, $0.27007 \times 7.48 = 2.020$ h, which also gives 9.59 a.m.)
[M1 $\frac{4}{x - 2}$ as $Q$'s share, M1 remaining share $\times$ $x$ for $P$'s working time, A1 9.59 a.m.]
Common wrong answers: 7 h 29 min in (b) (the time for $P$, not $Q$); 9.27 a.m. in (c) (the two machines' times swapped).
question.syllabus_check: 4052 only: a word problem (rates of work) leading to a fractional equation that reduces to a quadratic, solved by the quadratic formula, with a root rejected in context; time conversions between hours, minutes and clock times. No calculus, no inequalities, no content outside 4052.
question.originality_note: Topic tested before in our Sets only as a percentage profit-and-loss chain (Set 1 P2 Q2), a without-replacement probability (Set 1 P1 Q13), a quadratic sequence (Set 1 P1 Q25), a speed-time trapezium (Set 2 P1 Q19) and similar triangles (Set 2 P1 Q23); rates of work appear in no earlier Set. Against the real papers: GCE 2024 P2 Q6 is a two-stage speed journey; GCE 2018 P2 Q6 and GCE 2012 P2 Q8 are pumps with a stated DIFFERENCE of filling times and a 'together' follow-on; GCE 2016 P2 Q7 counts mugs painted at per-item times. Here the model is shares of ONE job done over DIFFERENT working times read from clock times (one machine breaks down, the other works through), both roots are positive so the rejection must be reasoned, (b) asks for the other machine's time rather than x, and (c) reverses the model to find a start time rather than a combined time. Part sequence [5, 3, 3] differs from Set 1 P2 Q2 [5, 2, 1, 3] and GCE 2024 P2 Q6 [5, 3, 1, 2]; no scaffold expressions are asked for.

answers.(b): 5 hours 29 minutes (x = 7.4767, rejecting x = 0.357 since x > 2)

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both 'shown'. Checked: P works 8.00-9.20 = 4/3 h, Q works 8.00-12.30 = 9/2 h; 4/(3x) + 9/(2(x-2)) = 1, times 6x(x-2): 8(x-2) + 27x = 6x^2 - 12x, so 6x^2 - 47x + 16 = 0. True show-that; the trap (Q counted only from 9.20, 19/6 h) gives 6x^2 - 39x + 16 = 0 and is caught by the printed target.

parts.label: (c)
parts.note: Both 9.59 a.m. Q's share 4/5.4767 = 0.73037, P works 0.26963 x 7.4767 = 2.0159 h, start 9:59.04. Robust to sensible rounding: x = 7.48 gives 9:58.8, Q's time taken as 5 h 29 min gives 9:58.5, both 9.59; only a 2 s.f. x = 7.5 drifts to 9.57.

verdict.key_verdict: The setter and the blind examiner agree on every part, and my own working confirms (a) shown, (b) 5 h 29 min, (c) 9.59 a.m.
fixes: Skills phrase 3 is not true of the question: machine Q does not 'work alone for 4 hours'. It works 4 hours in total, alone until P joins and then with P. Rewrite: 'reversed work-rate: machine P's working time found from the share of the order left after machine Q's 4 hours of work (Q works throughout, first alone, then with P), counted back from 12 noon to a start time'.

Light edit to SEAB register in the stem's first sentence: 'Every order that the factory receives is for the same number of paper bags, and each machine always works at its own constant rate.' -> 'Each order is for the same number of paper bags. Each machine works at its own constant rate.'
verdict.why: This is the P2 staple of a formed quadratic, shape [5, 3, 3], as the plan asked. Its model is new: shares of one job over different working times read off clock times, with Q working through P's breakdown. Every part holds a decision with a believable wrong answer: 6x^2 - 39x + 16, 7 h 29 min, 9.27 a.m. It is at least as demanding and clean as Set 1 P2 Q2. It is not a re-skin of GCE 2024 P2 Q6, whose situation and model differ, although it has the same four-part family shape and the same reason for rejecting a root (x - k < 0). Past pump questions (GCE 2012 P2 Q8, GCE 2018 P2 Q6) gave rates and a difference of times with expression rungs; this one does not.
verdict.session_note: 23 Sep: polish: fixes 1 (skills phrase 3) and 2 (stem wording). Answers unchanged; gates re-run.

question.stem:
A lighthouse, $L$, stands on a small island.
A ship sails in a straight line on a bearing of $038^\circ$ at a constant speed of 20 km/h.
At 10 00 the ship is at $A$ and $L$ is on a bearing of $062^\circ$ from the ship.
At 10 45 the ship is at $B$ and $L$ is due east of the ship.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Calculate the distance between the ship and $L$ at 10 45.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
The ship continues on the same course at the same speed.
Find the time at which the ship is closest to $L$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
At 10 45 a supply boat leaves $L$ and sails in a straight line at a constant speed to meet the ship.
When they meet, the supply boat has sailed the shortest possible distance.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.text: Find the bearing on which the supply boat sails.

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.text: Calculate the speed of the supply boat.

skills: interior angles of a triangle from a ship's course and two sightings of one point taken at different times, using the reversed course at the second position and a 'due east' sighting, then the sine rule for a side
closest approach of a moving ship: the foot of the perpendicular from the fixed point to the course, and the clock time it is reached from the distance along the course
shortest route to meet a moving ship: sail perpendicular to its course and choose the speed that arrives at the same moment
question.solution:
(a) From 10 00 to 10 45 is 45 minutes, so $AB = 20 \times \frac{45}{60} = 15$ km.
At $A$: angle $LAB = 062^\circ - 038^\circ = 24^\circ$.
At $B$: the bearing of $A$ from $B$ is $038^\circ + 180^\circ = 218^\circ$ and $L$ is due east of $B$ (bearing $090^\circ$), so angle $ABL = 218^\circ - 90^\circ = 128^\circ$.
Angle $ALB = 180^\circ - 24^\circ - 128^\circ = 28^\circ$.
Sine rule in triangle $ABL$: $\frac{BL}{\sin 24^\circ} = \frac{15}{\sin 28^\circ}$
$BL = \frac{15 \sin 24^\circ}{\sin 28^\circ} = 12.996 \ldots = 13.0$ km (3 s.f.)
(Taking angle $ABL$ as $90^\circ - 38^\circ = 52^\circ$, the angle between the course and $BL$, gives the wrong value $6.29$ km: the angle inside triangle $ABL$ at $B$ is between $BA$ and $BL$.)

(b) The ship is closest to $L$ at the point $X$ on its course where $LX$ is perpendicular to the course.
At $B$ the angle between the direction of travel ($038^\circ$) and $BL$ ($090^\circ$) is $90^\circ - 38^\circ = 52^\circ$, which is acute, so $X$ lies ahead of $B$ on the course.
In the right-angled triangle $BXL$: $BX = BL \cos 52^\circ = 12.996 \times \cos 52^\circ = 8.000 \ldots$ km.
Time to sail from $B$ to $X$ $= \frac{8.000}{20} = 0.4000$ h $= 24.0$ minutes.
The ship is closest to $L$ at 10 45 + 24 minutes $=$ 11 09.

(c)(i) The shortest distance from $L$ to the ship's course is the perpendicular distance $LX$, so the supply boat sails along $LX$ and meets the ship at $X$ at 11 09.
$LX$ is perpendicular to the course, so the bearing of $L$ from $X$ is $038^\circ + 90^\circ = 128^\circ$.
Bearing on which the supply boat sails (bearing of $X$ from $L$) $= 128^\circ + 180^\circ = 308^\circ$.
(Check: the bearing of $B$ from $L$ is $270^\circ$ and angle $BLX = 90^\circ - 52^\circ = 38^\circ$, so $270^\circ + 38^\circ = 308^\circ$.)

(c)(ii) $LX = BL \sin 52^\circ = 12.996 \times \sin 52^\circ = 10.24 \ldots$ km (or $LX = \sqrt{BL^2 - BX^2}$).
The boat leaves at 10 45 and reaches $X$ at 11 09, so it sails for 24 minutes $= 0.4$ h.
Speed $= \frac{10.24}{0.4} = 25.6$ km/h (3 s.f.)

question.solution:
(a)(i) When $x = 4.5$: $y = \frac{4.5^3}{2} - 3(4.5)^2 + 4(4.5) + 3 = 45.5625 - 60.75 + 18 + 3 = 5.8125 = 5.8$ (1 d.p.). [B1]

(a)(ii) Plot the 11 points $(0, 3)$, $(0.5, 4.3)$, $(1, 4.5)$, $(1.5, 3.9)$, $(2, 3)$, $(2.5, 2.1)$, $(3, 1.5)$, $(3.5, 1.7)$, $(4, 3)$, $(4.5, 5.8)$, $(5, 10.5)$ using 2 cm to 1 unit on the $x$-axis and 1 cm to 1 unit on the $y$-axis, and join them with a smooth curve. The curve rises to a maximum of about $4.5$ (between $x = 0.5$ and $x = 1$), falls to a minimum of about $1.5$ (just after $x = 3$), then rises steeply to $10.5$ at $x = 5$. [P2 for all 11 points correctly plotted (P1 for at least 9), C1 for a smooth curve through them]

(b) Rearrange so that one side is the curve that has been drawn.
$x^3 + 6x + 4 > 6x^2$
$x^3 - 6x^2 + 6x + 4 > 0$
Divide by 2: $\frac{x^3}{2} - 3x^2 + 3x + 2 > 0$
Add $x + 1$ to both sides: $\frac{x^3}{2} - 3x^2 + 4x + 3 > x + 1$.
So draw the line $y = x + 1$ (through $(0, 1)$, $(2, 3)$ and $(5, 6)$) and find where the curve is ABOVE the line. [B1 for $y = x + 1$]
The line meets the curve at $x = 2$ (the point $(2, 3)$) and at $x \approx 4.45$. [B1 for both $x$-values read, accept $4.4$ to $4.5$]
At $x = 0$ the curve ($y = 3$) is above the line ($y = 1$); between $x = 2$ and $x = 4.45$ the curve is below the line (e.g. at $x = 3$: $1.5 < 4$); after $x = 4.45$ it is above again (at $x = 5$: $10.5 > 6$).
Solution: $0 \le x < 2$ or $4.45 < x \le 5$. [A1, both intervals]
(Check: $x^3 - 6x^2 + 6x + 4 = (x - 2)(x^2 - 4x - 2)$, roots $x = 2$ and $x = 2 \pm \sqrt{6}$, i.e. $4.449$ and $-0.449$; the root $-0.449$ is outside $0 \le x \le 5$.)
Tempting wrong answers: $2 < x < 4.45$ (the region where the curve is below the line) or $x > 4.45$ only (missing the interval that starts at the end point $x = 0$).

(c)(i) The solutions of $\frac{x^3}{2} - 3x^2 + 4x + 3 = k$ are the $x$-coordinates of the points where the horizontal line $y = k$ meets the curve, and only the part of the curve for $0 \le x \le 5$ counts.
The line $y = k$ meets the drawn curve three times only while it cuts all three sections of the curve: the section from $(0, 3)$ up to the maximum, the section from the maximum down to the minimum, and the section from the minimum up to $(5, 10.5)$.
The first section only covers $3 \le y \le 4.5$, because the curve starts at $y = 3$ when $x = 0$.
So $3 \le k < 4.5$ (maximum read from the graph, accept $4.5$ to $4.6$). [B1 lower bound 3 (condone $<$), B1 upper bound with $<$]
At $k = 3$ there are exactly three solutions, $x = 0$, $2$ and $4$; for $k$ just below 3 the line meets the curve only twice, and at $k = 4.5$ (the maximum) only twice.
Tempting wrong answer: $1.5 < k < 4.5$, from the two turning values, ignoring that the curve begins at $y = 3$.

(c)(ii) $x^3 - 6x^2 + 8x = p$
Divide by 2: $\frac{x^3}{2} - 3x^2 + 4x = \frac{p}{2}$
Add 3: $\frac{x^3}{2} - 3x^2 + 4x + 3 = \frac{p}{2} + 3$.
So this is the equation of (c)(i) with $k = \frac{p}{2} + 3$, i.e. $p = 2k - 6$. [M1]
$3 \le k < 4.5$ gives $2(3) - 6 \le p < 2(4.5) - 6$, so $0 \le p < 3.1$ (accept $3.0$ to $3.2$ from the maximum read in (c)(i); exact value $3.08$). [A1]
(Check: $p = 0$ gives $x(x - 2)(x - 4) = 0$, which has exactly the three solutions $0$, $2$ and $4$ in the range.)
Tempting wrong answer: $-3 < p < 3$, from the turning values $1.5$ and $4.5$.

question.stem:
The diagram shows a circle, centre $O$.
$A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ are points on the circle.
$AC$ bisects angle $BAD$.
The tangent to the circle at $C$ meets $AD$ produced at $E$.
Angle $ABD = 40^\circ$ and angle $BDC = 34^\circ$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
Show that triangle $BCD$ is isosceles.
Give a reason for each statement you make.
parts.answer: Angle $BAC$ = angle $BDC = 34^\circ$ (angles in the same segment); angle $CAD$ = angle $BAC = 34^\circ$ ($AC$ bisects angle $BAD$); angle $CBD$ = angle $CAD = 34^\circ$ (angles in the same segment). So angle $CBD$ = angle $CDB$ and triangle $BCD$ is isosceles ($CB = CD$).

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
$BD = 12$ cm.
Calculate the area of quadrilateral $OBCD$.

parts.label: (c)

Find angle $AEC$.
Give a reason for each step of your working.

question.answer: (a) Proof: angle $CBD$ = angle $CAD$ = angle $BAC$ = angle $BDC = 34^\circ$, so triangle $BCD$ is isosceles. (b) $38.8$ cm$^2$. (c) $72^\circ$.
skills: prove the triangle opposite a bisected angle of a cyclic quadrilateral is isosceles by pairing angles in the same segment with the bisector
radius from a chord and the angle it subtends at the circumference (angle at the centre, perpendicular from the centre), then the area of the kite of radii OBCD, with no radius given

angle between the tangent at C and AD produced, linking the tangent to the angles inside the circle through tangent perpendicular to radius (OC perpendicular to BD from part (a), or the isosceles triangle OCD)

Four points on the circumference, labelled just outside the circle, placed at these positions about O (angles measured anticlockwise from the positive x-direction): A at 83 degrees (top, slightly right of the vertical), B at 227 degrees (lower left), C at 295 degrees (bottom right), D at 3 degrees (right). With O at the origin and the radius as 1 unit, the coordinates are A (0.122, 0.993), B (-0.682, -0.731), C (0.423, -0.906), D (0.999, 0.052). Draw as solid straight lines the four sides AB, BC, CD and DA of quadrilateral ABCD and both diagonals AC and BD. Extend AD beyond D as a solid straight line to the point E (1.447, -0.429), labelled E. Draw the tangent to the circle at C as a solid straight line from a point about 0.3 units beyond C on the lower-left side, through C, to E (E lies on this tangent, outside the circle, to the right of D and below it). question.solution:
(a)
Angle $BAC$ = angle $BDC = 34^\circ$ (angles in the same segment, on chord $BC$).
Angle $CAD$ = angle $BAC = 34^\circ$ ($AC$ bisects angle $BAD$).
Angle $CBD$ = angle $CAD = 34^\circ$ (angles in the same segment, on chord $CD$).
So angle $CBD$ = angle $CDB = 34^\circ$, and triangle $BCD$ is isosceles with $CB = CD$ (base angles equal).

(b)
Angle $BAD = 34^\circ + 34^\circ = 68^\circ$.
Angle $BOD = 2 \times 68^\circ = 136^\circ$ (angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference).
$OB = OD$ (radii), so the perpendicular from $O$ to $BD$ meets $BD$ at its midpoint $M$ and bisects angle $BOD$: $BM = 6$ cm and angle $BOM = 68^\circ$.
Radius $r = OB = \frac{6}{\sin 68^\circ} = 6.4712$ cm.
(Or: in isosceles triangle $OBD$, angle $OBD = \frac{180^\circ - 136^\circ}{2} = 22^\circ$, and $\frac{r}{\sin 22^\circ} = \frac{12}{\sin 136^\circ}$ gives $r = 6.4712$ cm.)
Angle $BOC = 2 \times$ angle $BAC = 68^\circ$ and angle $COD = 2 \times$ angle $CAD = 68^\circ$ (angle at the centre).
Area of $OBCD$ = area of triangle $OBC$ + area of triangle $OCD$
$= 2 \times \frac{1}{2} \times 6.4712^2 \times \sin 68^\circ$
$= 38.827$
$= 38.8$ cm$^2$ (3 s.f.).
(Check: $OC$ is perpendicular to $BD$ (see (c)), so area $= \frac{1}{2} \times OC \times BD = \frac{1}{2} \times 6.4712 \times 12 = 38.8$ cm$^2$; or area $BCD$ + area $OBD = \frac{1}{2} \times 7.2373^2 \times \sin 112^\circ + \frac{1}{2} \times 6.4712^2 \times \sin 136^\circ = 24.282 + 14.545 = 38.8$ cm$^2$, with $CB = \frac{6}{\cos 34^\circ} = 7.2373$ cm.)
Tempting errors: treating $BD$ as a diameter ($r = 6$, area $33.4$ cm$^2$), or taking angle $BOD = 2 \times 34^\circ$ ($r = 10.7$ cm).

(c)
Method 1:
$CB = CD$ (part (a)) and $OB = OD$ (radii), so $C$ and $O$ both lie on the perpendicular bisector of the chord $BD$ (the perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the centre). Hence $OC$ is perpendicular to $BD$.
Angle $OCE = 90^\circ$ (tangent is perpendicular to the radius).
So $CE$ is parallel to $BD$ (both are perpendicular to $OC$).
Angle $ADB = 180^\circ - 68^\circ - 40^\circ = 72^\circ$ (angle sum of triangle $ABD$).
Angle $AEC$ = angle $ADB = 72^\circ$ (corresponding angles, $EC$ parallel to $DB$).
Method 2:
Angle $COD = 2 \times$ angle $CBD = 68^\circ$ (angle at the centre); angle $OCD = \frac{180^\circ - 68^\circ}{2} = 56^\circ$ (base angles of isosceles triangle $OCD$).
Angle $DCE = 90^\circ - 56^\circ = 34^\circ$ (tangent is perpendicular to the radius).
Angle $ABC = 40^\circ + 34^\circ = 74^\circ$, so angle $ADC = 180^\circ - 74^\circ = 106^\circ$ (angles in opposite segments are supplementary).
Angle $CDE = 180^\circ - 106^\circ = 74^\circ$ (adjacent angles on a straight line).
Angle $AEC = 180^\circ - 34^\circ - 74^\circ = 72^\circ$ (angle sum of triangle $CDE$).

Mark scheme: (a) B1 one same-segment pair with reason; B1 the bisector step and the conclusion $CBD = CDB$. (b) M1 angle $BOD = 136^\circ$ or angle $BOC = 68^\circ$; M1 $r = \frac{6}{\sin 68^\circ}$ or equivalent; M1 area as $2 \times \frac{1}{2} r^2 \sin 68^\circ$ or $\frac{1}{2} \times r \times 12$ or equivalent; A1 $38.8$. (c) B1 angle $DCE = 34^\circ$, or $CE \parallel BD$, with correct reason(s); B1 angle $CDE = 74^\circ$ (angles in opposite segments are supplementary, or exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral, with adjacent angles on a straight line) or angle $ADB = 72^\circ$ (angle sum of triangle $ABD$); B1 $72^\circ$ with the final reason.
Note on (c): angle $DCE$ = angle $CAD = 34^\circ$ (alternate segment theorem / tangent-chord theorem) is accepted: it is a valid theorem, although not required by 4052. Any valid route with a reason at each step scores 3/3.

No alternate segment theorem is required (a candidate who uses it for angle $DCE = 34^\circ$ still reaches $72^\circ$), no radians, no arc or sector work, no part of 5 or more marks.
question.originality_note: New configuration: a diagonal that bisects an angle of a cyclic quadrilateral, so the opposite vertex is the midpoint of its arc (isosceles triangle, kite of radii, tangent parallel to the chord). Earlier Sets tested angles in the same segment only as a 2-mark numeric chase at a chord intersection (Set 1 P1 Q9), equal tangents and an incircle (Set 1 P2 Q5), the angle in a semicircle by construction (Set 2 P1 Q7) and, in Set 2 P1 Q13, a tangent where the angle at the external point is GIVEN and angles inside are found; here the angle at the external point is FOUND, most directly through the parallel the arc midpoint forces. The radius is recovered from a chord and an angle at the circumference through the angle at the centre (Set 1 P2 Q8 found a radius from a chord and a height by Pythagoras), and the paper's opposite-segments property appears for the first time across the Sets. Not a re-skin of GCE 2024 P2 Q8(a) (equal chords, midpoints, RHS congruence), GCE 2003 P2 Q5 (parallel chords, isosceles triangle at the chord intersection) or GCE 2005 P2 Q3 (a bisector with a diameter).

answers.(b): 38.8 cm² (angle BOD = 2 × 68° = 136°, r = 6/sin 68° = 6.471 cm; OBCD is a kite with OC ⊥ BD, area = ½ × OC × BD = 6r = 38.83 cm²; equivalently 14.54 + 24.28)

question.stem: $A$ is the point $(-3, 2)$, $B$ is the point $(0, -2)$ and $C$ is the point $(5, -2)$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Calculate angle $ABC$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
The point $D$ lies on the line $y = x + 2$ and is the same distance from $A$ as it is from $C$.
Find the coordinates of $D$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Explain why $ABCD$ has exactly one line of symmetry, and find the equation of this line.
parts.answer: $BA = BC = 5$ and $DA = DC = \sqrt{65}$, but $AB \ne AD$, so $ABCD$ is a kite and not a rhombus; its only line of symmetry is the diagonal $BD$, $y = 2x - 2$

parts.label: (d)
parts.text:
The point $P$ lies on $BD$.
The area of the quadrilateral $ABCP$ is $30$ units$^2$.
Find the coordinates of $P$.

question.answer: (a) $126.9^\circ$  (b) $(4, 6)$  (c) $BA = BC = 5$, $DA = DC = \sqrt{65}$, $AB \ne AD$: a kite, not a rhombus, so the only line of symmetry is $BD$; $y = 2x - 2$  (d) $(3, 4)$
skills: obtuse angle at a vertex between a horizontal side and a slanted side from coordinates: 180 degrees - tan^-1(4/3) or the cosine rule (trap: the acute 53.1 degrees)
point on a given line equidistant from two points: equate the two squared lengths so the squared terms cancel to a linear equation

explain from its side lengths why a quadrilateral has exactly one line of symmetry (a kite, not a rhombus: BA = BC, DA = DC, AB != AD, so the axis is BD, not AC) and find the equation of that diagonal
locate a point on the axis of symmetry from the area of a symmetric quadrilateral: area ABCP = 2 x area BCP on the horizontal base BC (or BP : BD = 30 : 40)
question.solution:
(a) $BC$ lies along the line $y = -2$. Let $F$ be the point $(-3, -2)$, directly below $A$, on the line $CB$ produced.
In the right-angled triangle $ABF$, $AF = 2 - (-2) = 4$ and $BF = 0 - (-3) = 3$.
$\tan \angle ABF = \frac{4}{3}$, so $\angle ABF = 53.13^\circ$.
$F$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of $B$ on the line $y = -2$, so angle $ABC = 180^\circ - 53.13^\circ = 126.87^\circ = 126.9^\circ$ (1 d.p.).
[Alternative: $AB = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$, $BC = 5$, $AC^2 = 8^2 + 4^2 = 80$; $\cos ABC = \frac{25 + 25 - 80}{2 \times 5 \times 5} = -0.6$, angle $ABC = 126.9^\circ$.]
M1 for $\tan^{-1}\frac{4}{3}$ (or the cosine rule with $AC^2 = 80$), A1 $126.9^\circ$. The tempting wrong answer is the acute angle $53.1^\circ$.

(b) $D$ lies on $y = x + 2$, so let $D$ be $(d, d + 2)$.
$DA^2 = (d + 3)^2 + (d + 2 - 2)^2 = (d + 3)^2 + d^2$
$DC^2 = (d - 5)^2 + (d + 2 + 2)^2 = (d - 5)^2 + (d + 4)^2$
$DA = DC$ gives $(d + 3)^2 + d^2 = (d - 5)^2 + (d + 4)^2$
$d^2 + 6d + 9 + d^2 = d^2 - 10d + 25 + d^2 + 8d + 16$
$6d + 9 = -2d + 41$
$8d = 32$, so $d = 4$.
$D = (4, 6)$. Check: $DA^2 = 7^2 + 4^2 = 65$ and $DC^2 = 1^2 + 8^2 = 65$.
M1 for $DA^2$ or $DC^2$ in terms of $d$, M1 for equating and simplifying to a linear equation, A1 $(4, 6)$.

(c) $BA = \sqrt{(-3 - 0)^2 + (2 + 2)^2} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5$ and $BC = 5 - 0 = 5$, so $BA = BC = 5$.
From (b), $DA = DC = \sqrt{65}$.
So $ABCD$ has two pairs of equal adjacent sides, meeting at $B$ and at $D$: it is a kite. It is not a rhombus, since $AB = 5$ but $AD = \sqrt{65}$, so $AB \ne AD$.
A kite that is not a rhombus has exactly one line of symmetry, the diagonal through the vertices where its equal sides meet: here $BD$. ($A$ and $C$ are reflections of each other in $BD$; $AC$ is not a line of symmetry, since $B$ and $D$ are not equidistant from $A$.)
Gradient of $BD = \frac{6 - (-2)}{4 - 0} = \frac{8}{4} = 2$, and the line passes through $B(0, -2)$, so its $y$-intercept is $-2$.
Line of symmetry: $y = 2x - 2$.
B1 for $BA = BC = 5$ and $DA = DC = \sqrt{65}$ with $AB \ne AD$ (a kite, not a rhombus, so the only line of symmetry is the diagonal $BD$), M1 gradient of $BD = 2$, A1 $y = 2x - 2$. An equation of $BD$ given without the reason scores M1 A1 only.

(d) $P$ lies on $BD$, i.e. on $y = 2x - 2$ between $B$ and $D$, so $P = (p, 2p - 2)$ with $0 \le p \le 4$.
$A$ and $C$ are reflections of each other in $BD$ and $P$ is on $BD$, so triangles $ABP$ and $CBP$ are congruent and area of $ABCP = 2 \times$ area of triangle $BCP$.
$BC$ is horizontal, of length 5, and the height of $P$ above $BC$ is $(2p - 2) - (-2) = 2p$.
Area of triangle $BCP = \frac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 2p = 5p$, so area of $ABCP = 10p$.
$10p = 30$, so $p = 3$ and $2p - 2 = 4$.
$P = (3, 4)$.
[Alternative: area of $ABCD = 2 \times$ area of triangle $BCD = 2 \times \frac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 8 = 40$. For $P$ on $BD$ the area of $ABCP$ is proportional to $BP$, so $BP : BD = 30 : 40 = 3 : 4$ and $\overrightarrow{BP} = \frac{3}{4}\overrightarrow{BD} = \frac{3}{4}\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 8 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$, giving $P = (0 + 3, -2 + 6) = (3, 4)$.]
Check: area of $ABCP = \frac{1}{2} \times AC \times BP = \frac{1}{2} \times \sqrt{80} \times \sqrt{45} = \frac{1}{2} \times 60 = 30$.
M1 for area $ABCP = 2 \times$ area $BCP$ (or area $ABCP$ : area $ABCD = BP : BD$), M1 for $\frac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 2p = 15$ (or $BP = \frac{3}{4}BD$), A1 $(3, 4)$. The tempting wrong decision, area of triangle $BCP = 30$, gives $(6, 10)$, which is beyond $D$ and not on $BD$.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 only. Coordinate geometry: length of a segment from coordinates, gradient from two points, equation y = mx + c (G7.1-7.4, 'geometric problems involving coordinates'). Trigonometric ratios in a right-angled triangle and an obtuse angle as 180 degrees minus an acute angle (or the cosine rule). Area of a triangle as half base times height; congruent triangles by symmetry. No midpoint formula, no perpendicular-gradient condition, no shoelace formula and no circle equation is needed anywhere; every equation (the linear equation in d, the area equation in p) is formed by the candidate without a prompt.
question.originality_note: Not a re-skin of any exemplar or earlier Set. Numbers are new: A(-3, 2), B(0, -2), C(5, -2), D(4, 6), P(3, 4).

answers.(c): BA = BC = 5 and DA = DC = √65, so ABCD is a kite (not a rhombus since AB ≠ AD); B and D lie on the perpendicular bisector of AC, so the only line of symmetry is BD: y = 2x − 2

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both 126.9 degrees. Checked: BA = (-3, 4), BC = (5, 0), cos ABC = -15/25 = -0.6, angle 126.87 = 126.9 degrees (or 180 - tan^-1(4/3)). Tempting wrong answer 53.1 degrees.

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Both (4, 6). Checked: D = (d, d + 2); DA^2 = (d + 3)^2 + d^2, DC^2 = (d - 5)^2 + (d + 4)^2; the squared terms cancel to 6d + 9 = -2d + 41, d = 4; DA^2 = DC^2 = 65.

parts.label: (c)
parts.note: Both y = 2x - 2. Checked: BA = BC = 5 and DA = DC = sqrt(65), AB != AD, so ABCD is a kite (convex, vertices in order) and its only line of symmetry is BD; gradient 8/4 = 2 through B(0, -2). (This line is also the perpendicular bisector of AC.)

parts.label: (d)
parts.note: Both (3, 4). Checked: P = (p, 2p - 2), area ABCP = 2 x area BCP = 2 x (1/2)(5)(2p) = 10p = 30, p = 3, on segment BD (0 <= p <= 4). Shoelace on A, B, C, P gives 60/2 = 30; area ABCD = 40. Trap: area BCP = 30 gives (6, 10), beyond D.

verdict.key_verdict: The setter and the blind examiner agree on every part, and my own working confirms all four answers: 126.9 degrees, (4, 6), y = 2x - 2, (3, 4).
fixes: (c): make the kite reasoning carry the marks: 'Explain why ABCD has exactly one line of symmetry and find its equation. [3]' (B1 BA = BC = 5 and DA = DC = sqrt(65) with AB != AD, so a kite and not a rhombus; M1 gradient of BD = 2; A1 y = 2x - 2). As set, once BD is picked from a sketch the equation is a read-off (B is the y-intercept), and a candidate who does (b) by the perpendicular bisector of AC (midpoint (1, 0), gradient 2: outside 4052, but common among A-Math candidates) has already written y = 2x - 2, so (c) pays 3 marks for no new idea. Requiring the justification keeps one mark that the A-Math route does not earn.

skills: add the skill (a) tests: the obtuse angle at B between a horizontal side and a slanted side, 180 - tan^-1(4/3) or the cosine rule (trap 53.1 degrees). The three phrases given are true of the question and specific.

The parts build on one object: D from equidistance, the kite's axis, then P on the axis from an area by symmetry. question.stem:
A fish farm has two ponds, $P$ and $Q$. A sample of 15 fish is netted from pond $P$ and a sample of 19 fish is netted from pond $Q$. The length of each fish is measured in centimetres.
The back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram shows the results.
$\begin{array}{r|c|l} \text{Pond } P & & \text{Pond } Q \\ 8 & 1 & 1 \\ 8\;\;7\;\;6\;\;4\;\;3\;\;1 & 2 & 7\;\;8\;\;9\;\;9 \\ 9\;\;7\;\;6\;\;4\;\;3\;\;1\;\;0 & 3 & 0\;\;1\;\;1\;\;2\;\;2\;\;3\;\;3\;\;4\;\;4\;\;5\;\;6\;\;6\;\;7\;\;8 \\ 1 & 4 & \end{array}$
Key: $4 \mid 2 \mid 7$ means a length of 24 cm for pond $P$ and a length of 27 cm for pond $Q$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: (i) $P$: 12 cm, $Q$: 6 cm; (ii) No: $Q$'s range (27 cm) is large only because of the single 11 cm fish, and its interquartile range (6 cm) is smaller than $P$'s (12 cm); (iii) 31.5 cm

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.text: Find the interquartile range of the lengths of the fish from each pond.

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.text:
Mei says that the lengths of the fish from pond $Q$ are more spread out than those from pond $P$, because the range for pond $Q$ is greater.
Is she correct? Give a reason, using figures to support your answer.
subparts.answer: No. The range for pond $Q$ ($38 - 11 = 27$ cm, against $41 - 18 = 23$ cm for pond $P$) is large only because of the one extreme value, a fish of length 11 cm; the other 18 fish from pond $Q$ lie between 27 cm and 38 cm. The interquartile range for pond $Q$ (6 cm) is smaller than that for pond $P$ (12 cm), so the middle half of the lengths from pond $Q$ is less spread out.

subparts.label: (iii)
subparts.text:
The 34 fish in the two samples are put together.
Find the median length of these 34 fish.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
A fish is ready for sale if its length is at least 30 cm.
Two fish are chosen at random, without replacement, from the sample from pond $P$. One fish is chosen at random from the sample from pond $Q$.
Find the probability that exactly two of these three fish are ready for sale.

question.answer: (a)(i) 12 cm (pond $P$), 6 cm (pond $Q$); (a)(ii) No: the range for $Q$ is large only because of the one 11 cm fish; its interquartile range (6 cm) is smaller than $P$'s (12 cm), so $Q$ is less spread out; (a)(iii) 31.5 cm; (b) $\frac{44}{95}$
skills: interquartile ranges read from a back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram with samples of different sizes (15 and 19), then used to judge a claim about spread that rests on a range inflated by one extreme value
median of two samples combined, found as the 17th and 18th values of the merged back-to-back data rather than the mean of the two separate medians
probability that exactly two of three items meet a condition when two are drawn without replacement from one sample and one from a different sample: three cases according to which item fails
question.solution:
(a)(i) Pond $P$ (15 lengths, in order): 18, 21, 23, 24, 26, 27, 28, 30, 31, 33, 34, 36, 37, 39, 41 (the leaves on the left are read outwards from the stem).
Median $=$ 8th value $= 30$. Lower quartile $=$ 4th value $= 24$, upper quartile $=$ 12th value $= 36$.
Interquartile range for $P = 36 - 24 = 12$ cm. [B1]
Pond $Q$ (19 lengths, in order): 11, 27, 28, 29, 29, 30, 31, 31, 32, 32, 33, 33, 34, 34, 35, 36, 36, 37, 38.
Median $=$ 10th value $= 32$. Lower quartile $=$ 5th value $= 29$, upper quartile $=$ 15th value $= 35$.
Interquartile range for $Q = 35 - 29 = 6$ cm. [B1]
(a)(ii) Range for $P = 41 - 18 = 23$ cm; range for $Q = 38 - 11 = 27$ cm, so the range for $Q$ is greater, as Mei says.
But Mei is not correct. The range for $Q$ is large only because of one fish of length 11 cm, which is much shorter than every other fish in that sample: the other 18 fish from pond $Q$ lie between 27 cm and 38 cm (a spread of only 11 cm).
The interquartile range is not affected by this one extreme value, and it is 6 cm for $Q$ against 12 cm for $P$, so the middle half of the lengths from pond $Q$ is LESS spread out.
[B1 — No, with a reason supported by a figure: EITHER the one extreme value 11 cm (the other 18 fish lie between 27 cm and 38 cm), OR the interquartile ranges compared, 6 cm for $Q$ < 12 cm for $P$. A reason with no figure, or "No" alone, scores 0.]
(a)(iii) There are 34 lengths, so the median is the mean of the 17th and 18th values of the combined data.
Combined counts by stem: stem 1: $1 + 1 = 2$ (running total 2); stem 2: $6 + 4 = 10$ (running total 12); so the 17th and 18th values are the 5th and 6th smallest lengths on stem 3.
Stem 3, both ponds together, in order: 30, 30, 31, 31, 31, 32, 32, 33, 33, 33, ... so the 5th is 31 and the 6th is 32. [M1]
Median $= \frac{31 + 32}{2} = 31.5$ cm. [A1]
(The mean of the two separate medians, $\frac{30 + 32}{2} = 31$ cm, is NOT the median of the combined data.)
(b) Ready for sale (at least 30 cm): pond $P$: 30, 31, 33, 34, 36, 37, 39, 41, so 8 of the 15 are ready and 7 are not; pond $Q$: 19 − 5 = 14 are ready (the 5 not ready are 11, 27, 28, 29, 29).
Exactly two ready means exactly one of the three fish is not ready. There are three cases.
First $P$ fish not ready, second $P$ fish ready, $Q$ fish ready: $\frac{7}{15} \times \frac{8}{14} \times \frac{14}{19} = \frac{784}{3990}$
First $P$ fish ready, second $P$ fish not ready, $Q$ fish ready: $\frac{8}{15} \times \frac{7}{14} \times \frac{14}{19} = \frac{784}{3990}$ [M1 for one correct product of three]
Both $P$ fish ready, $Q$ fish not ready: $\frac{8}{15} \times \frac{7}{14} \times \frac{5}{19} = \frac{280}{3990}$
Probability $= \frac{784 + 784 + 280}{3990} = \frac{1848}{3990} = \frac{44}{95}$ (0.463 to 3 s.f.). [M1 for adding all three cases, A1]
(Counting the two $P$ fish in only one order gives $\frac{4}{15}$, which is wrong.)
question.syllabus_check: 4052 data handling and analysis: stem-and-leaf diagrams (back-to-back), median, quartiles, interquartile range, range, comparing two distributions in context; probability: combined events, with and without replacement. No grouped data, no calculator statistics mode needed, nothing outside 4052.
question.originality_note: New situation (lengths of fish sampled from two ponds, a 30 cm ready-for-sale threshold) and a display no earlier Set has used (a back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram). Set 1 P2 Q7 took the mean and standard deviation from a grouped cumulative frequency table, explained what the grouped table cannot show and why a smaller mean need not mean fewer refunds, and found P(both of two from one pool); Set 2 P1 Q25 found an unknown frequency from a mean and tested an upper-quartile claim; Set 1 P1 Q4 recovered a missing value from a median; Set 2 P1 Q11 was a two-stage die game. Here the skills are different: judging a claim about spread that rests on the range when one value is extreme (range versus interquartile range), the median of two samples merged (trap: the mean of the two medians, 31), and a three-fish probability drawn from TWO different samples, two without replacement from one (trap: 4/15 when the order within pond P is ignored). Real stem-and-leaf questions (GCE 2019 P2 Q9, GCE 2018 P1 Q19, GCE 2016 P2 Q9, GCE 2010 P1 Q18) ask for medians, ranges, percentages and verbal comparisons, none of these three skills; GCE 2024 P2 Q7(b)(iii) draws three from a single pool.

answers.(a)(i): Pond P: Q1 = 24, Q3 = 36, IQR = 12 cm; Pond Q: Q1 = 29, Q3 = 35, IQR = 6 cm
answers.(a)(ii): No. Range Q = 38 - 11 = 27 cm > range P = 41 - 18 = 23 cm, but the range of Q is inflated by the extreme value 11 cm. IQR of Q (6 cm) is smaller than IQR of P (12 cm), so the lengths from pond Q are less spread out.
answers.(a)(iii): 31.5 cm (mean of the 17th and 18th values, 31 and 32)

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.note: Both give P: Q1 = 24, Q3 = 36, IQR 12 cm; Q: Q1 = 29, Q3 = 35, IQR 6 cm. Checked: P ordered 18 … 41 (15 values), Q ordered 11 … 38 (19 values); the halves method and the (n+1)/4 positions (4th/12th for P, 5th/15th for Q) give the same quartiles, so the answer does not depend on the convention a school teaches.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.note: Both say that Q's range (38 - 11 = 27 against P's 23) is inflated by the single 11 cm fish, and that Q's IQR (6) is half of P's (12). The same B1 fact in the same words.

parts.label: (a)(iii)
parts.note: Both give 31.5 cm. Checked: 2 values on stem 1 and 10 on stem 2 make 12, so the 17th and 18th are the 5th and 6th on stem 3 of the merged data (30, 30, 31, 31, 31, 32, …), which are 31 and 32. The tempting wrong answer, the mean of the two medians (30 + 32)/2 = 31, is a believable number.

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Both give 44/95. Checked: P has 8 ready (≥ 30, including the 30) and 7 not; Q has 14 ready and 5 not. 2(8/15)(7/14)(14/19) + (8/15)(7/14)(5/19) = 112/285 + 20/285 = 132/285 = 44/95. Counting the pond-P pair in one order only gives exactly 4/15, a tidy wrong answer. The inclusive 'at least 30 cm' also matters, because both samples contain a 30.

verdict.key_verdict: The setter's key and the blind examiner agree on every part, and I re-derived every value (IQRs 12 and 6, combined median 31.5, probability 44/95); the key is right.
fixes: (a)(ii) is telegraphed. The stem states the conclusion ('Explain why this does not mean …'), and (a)(i) has just handed the candidate the IQRs to quote. Hand the decision over in SEAB's register instead, e.g. 'Mei says that the lengths of the fish from pond Q are more spread out than those from pond P, because the range for pond Q is greater. Is she correct? Give a reason, using figures to support your answer. [1]'. The mark scheme should accept either the 11 cm extreme value with the other 18 fish lying within 27–38 cm, or the IQR comparison 6 < 12, and must require a figure.

(a)(i) [2] is a plain routine opener. The moderator's test allows it, but the only thing it adds is reading pond P's leaves outwards. That is acceptable. It needs no change, provided (a)(ii) is reworded as above so the question carries its reasoning mark on its own.
verdict.why: This is a real 4052 P2 statistics-and-probability question. A back-to-back display with unequal samples feeds a range-versus-IQR judgement, a merged median with a believable trap (31), and an exactly-two-of-three probability across two samples with a case split and a tidy trap (4/15). That puts 6 of its 8 marks on decisions, which is at the 2024/25 standard (compare GCE 2024 P2 Q7(b)(iii) [3]). It is not a re-skin of any 2024/25 question or exemplar. It is also not a repeat of Set 1 P2 Q7: a different display and different measures, and its probability part is a three-case, two-source model where Set 1's was the single product P(both). Beside Set 1 P2 Q7 it matches on clean numbers, context doing real work (the 11 cm fish, the inclusive 30 cm threshold) and parts that build. question.stem:
The diagram shows a belt stretched tightly around two circular pulleys in a machine.
The larger pulley has centre $A$ and radius 25 cm. The smaller pulley has centre $B$ and radius 10 cm.
$AB = 39$ cm.
The straight parts of the belt, $PQ$ and $RS$, are tangents to both pulleys.
$PQ$ touches the larger pulley at $P$ and the smaller pulley at $Q$.
$RS$ touches the larger pulley at $R$ and the smaller pulley at $S$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Show that angle $PAB = 1.176$ radians, correct to 3 decimal places.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Calculate the length of the belt.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
The larger pulley turns at 150 revolutions per minute.
The belt does not slip on either pulley.
Calculate the time, in seconds, that it takes a point on the belt to make one complete circuit.

skills: angle between a radius and the line of centres found by building the right-angled triangle on a common external tangent of two circles (radii perpendicular to the tangent, side = difference of the radii)
length of a belt round two pulleys: two tangent lengths plus the arcs of contact, a reflex angle $2\pi - 2\theta$ on the larger pulley but only $2\theta$ on the smaller one, in radians
belt speed equal to the rim speed of the driving pulley (revolutions per minute to cm per second) to time one circuit of the belt
question.figure_description: Side view of two circles drawn to scale (1 unit = 1 cm). Larger circle: centre A at (0, 0), radius 25, on the LEFT. Smaller circle: centre B at (39, 0), radius 10, on the RIGHT, so AB is horizontal and the circles do not touch (gap of 4 between (25, 0) and (29, 0)). The belt is drawn as a THICK line made of four pieces: (1) the straight upper segment from P = (9.62, 23.08) on the larger circle to Q = (42.85, 9.23) on the smaller circle; (2) the straight lower segment from R = (9.62, -23.08) on the larger circle to S = (42.85, -9.23) on the smaller circle; (3) the MAJOR arc of the larger circle from P anticlockwise over the top, through the leftmost point (-25, 0), round to R; (4) the MINOR arc of the smaller circle from Q clockwise through the rightmost point (49, 0) round to S. The remaining parts of the two circles (the arc of the larger circle from P to R through (25, 0), facing B, and the arc of the smaller circle from Q to S through (29, 0), facing A) are drawn as thin lines, so both pulleys appear as complete circles. Thin straight lines: the radius AP, the radius BQ and the line of centres AB (AB may be dashed). A and B are marked as small dots at the centres. Label the points A, B, P, Q, R and S with letters only. Do NOT write any lengths, radii or angles on the diagram, do NOT mark right angles, and do NOT draw any line through B parallel to PQ: angle PAB, the length PQ and the length of the belt must not appear.
question.solution:
(a) A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, so $AP \perp PQ$ and $BQ \perp PQ$; hence $AP$ is parallel to $BQ$.
Draw the line through $B$ parallel to $QP$, meeting $AP$ at $X$. Then $PQBX$ is a rectangle, so $XP = BQ = 10$ cm, $BX = PQ$ and angle $AXB = 90^\circ$.
$AX = AP - XP = 25 - 10 = 15$ cm.   [M1]
In right-angled triangle $AXB$: $\cos \angle PAB = \frac{AX}{AB} = \frac{15}{39}$   [M1]
angle $PAB = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{15}{39}\right) = 1.17600\ldots = 1.176$ radians (3 d.p.)   [A1]

(b) $PQ = BX = \sqrt{39^2 - 15^2} = \sqrt{1296} = 36$ cm; by symmetry about $AB$, $RS = 36$ cm.   [M1]
The belt wraps the larger pulley along the major arc $PR$, on the side away from $B$.
Reflex angle $PAR = 2\pi - 2(1.176) = 3.9312$ radians   [M1]
Major arc $PR = 25 \times 3.9312 = 98.280$ cm.
Since $AP$ is parallel to $BQ$, angle $QBA = \pi - 1.176 = 1.9656$ radians (co-interior angles).
The belt wraps the smaller pulley along the minor arc $QS$, on the side away from $A$.
Angle $QBS$ (on the side away from $A$) $= 2\pi - 2(\pi - 1.176) = 2(1.176) = 2.352$ radians   [M1]
Minor arc $QS = 10 \times 2.352 = 23.52$ cm.
Length of belt $= 36 + 36 + 98.280 + 23.52$   [M1]
$= 193.80 = 194$ cm (3 s.f.)   [A1]
(Taking a semicircle on each pulley gives the wrong value $72 + 35\pi = 182$ cm; swapping the two angles gives $170$ cm.)

(c) The belt does not slip, so the belt moves at the same speed as a point on the rim of the larger pulley.
Speed of belt $= 150 \times 2\pi \times 25 = 7500\pi$ cm per minute $= 125\pi = 392.70$ cm/s   [M1]
Time for one complete circuit $= \frac{193.80}{392.70} = 0.49351 = 0.494$ s (3 s.f.)   [A1]
(Using the radius of the smaller pulley gives the wrong value 1.23 s.)
question.syllabus_check: Inside 4052: tangent perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact (properties of circles), parallel lines (co-interior angles), cosine ratio in a right-angled triangle with the angle in radians, Pythagoras' theorem, arc length $s = r\theta$ with $\theta$ in radians including a reflex angle, and speed as distance over time with a conversion of units. No calculus, no trigonometric identities, no 3-D work, nothing outside the 4052 syllabus.
question.originality_note: No belt, pulley or common-tangent question appears anywhere in the GCE corpus (2002-2025) or in any earlier Set. Set 1 P2 Q8 found a circle's radius from a chord and a height inside a road tunnel, then an arc, a segment-plus-rectangle area and a bus-clearance check; Set 2 P1 Q9 eliminated the angle between the arc-length and sector-area formulas; Set 1 P1 Q2 scaled a sector by an area factor. This question tests different skills: an angle from the right-angled triangle hidden in a common tangent of two circles, arcs of contact that are a reflex angle on one circle and an acute-based angle on the other, and a rim-speed rate. It shares no situation or part sequence with GCE 2024 P2 Q8(b) (two intersecting circles, shaded area via the sine rule) or GCE 2025 P2 Q6(a) (radians in the sine and cosine rules in a quadrilateral).

answers.(b): 194 cm (PQ = RS = √(39² − 15²) = 36; major arc on larger pulley = 25(2π − 2×1.176) = 98.28; minor arc on smaller pulley = 10(2×1.176) = 23.52; total = 72 + 98.28 + 23.52 = 193.80 ≈ 194 cm)

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both: AP and BQ are both perpendicular to PQ, so the right-angled triangle on AB has side 25 - 10 = 15 and cos PAB = 15/39 = 5/13, giving angle PAB = 1.17601 = 1.176 rad (checked: tan PAB = 36/15 = 2.4, arctan 2.4 = 1.17601). The printed target is true, and the construction is not drawn, so the candidate must build it.

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Both 194 cm. Checked: PQ = RS = sqrt(39^2 - 15^2) = 36; reflex angle on the larger pulley 2pi - 2(1.17601) = 3.93117, arc 98.279; angle on the smaller pulley 2(1.17601) = 2.35201 (parallel radii, co-interior angles), arc 23.520; total 72 + 98.279 + 23.520 = 193.80 = 194 cm. Using the rounded 1.176 changes nothing (193.80). Tempting wrong answers: 72 + 35pi = 182 (semicircles) and 170 (angles swapped).

parts.label: (c)
parts.note: Both 0.494 s. Checked: belt speed = rim speed of the larger pulley = 150 x 2pi x 25 = 7500pi cm/min = 392.70 cm/s; 193.80 / 392.70 = 0.4935 = 0.494 s. Tempting wrong answers: 0.4 s (one circuit taken as one revolution of the pulley) and 1.23 s (the smaller radius).

verdict.key_verdict: The setter and the blind examiner agree on every part (1.176 rad shown, 194 cm, 0.494 s), and my own working confirms all three.
verdict.why: All 10 marks sit in parts where the candidate decides the method: (a) building the triangle on the common tangent (side = difference of the radii) with the construction left undrawn, a show-that that gates (b); (b) a 5-mark chain (tangent length, reflex arc 2pi - 2theta on the larger pulley, only 2theta on the smaller one from the parallel radii) with believable wrong totals of 182 and 170; (c) rim speed as belt speed, with 0.4 s as the trap. The numbers are clean (the 15-36-39 triple), the wording is SEAB's, and no belt or common-tangent question appears in the corpus or any earlier Set. It matches Set 1 P2 Q8 in weight and polish. It shares only the generic P2 show-that-then-build shape with that question, not its situation (a tunnel) or its skills (radius from a chord and height, segment area, clearance), and no skill overlaps Q1, Q2 or Q7 of this paper. All gates passed.

question.stem:
A music festival is held in a park. Many people travel to the festival by train and then take a shuttle bus from the MRT station to the park. The organisers use the information below to plan the shuttle buses.

Last year's festival
The table shows the number of people who arrived at the station to take a shuttle bus in each hour.
$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Time of arrival} & \text{2 pm to 3 pm} & \text{3 pm to 4 pm} & \text{4 pm to 5 pm} & \text{5 pm to 6 pm} & \text{6 pm to 7 pm} \\ \hline \text{Number of people} & 450 & 1050 & 1600 & 2350 & 1550 \\ \hline \end{array}$

Buses for hire
$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Type of bus} & \text{Maximum number of passengers} & \text{Time for one round trip} & \text{Hire charge for the day} \\ \hline \text{Single-deck} & 60 & 20 \text{ minutes} & \$450 \\ \hline \text{Double-deck} & 100 & 30 \text{ minutes} & \$490 \\ \hline \end{array}$
A round trip is from the station to the park and back to the station, including the time for passengers to get on and off the bus.

The organisers assume that
• people arrive at the station at a steady rate during each hour,
• the buses run continuously from 2 pm, leaving the station one at a time at equal intervals, so that whenever people are waiting, the buses take them away from the station at a steady rate,
• each bus carries as many people as possible on each trip.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
Last year, the organisers hired 10 single-deck buses. There was no one waiting at the station at 2 pm.
Find the number of people waiting at the station for a shuttle bus at 7 pm.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
This year, the organisers expect $20\%$ more people than last year to arrive at the station in each hour.
So that the buses can run to a regular timetable, the organisers will hire buses of one type only. They need enough buses so that, in every hour, the buses can carry at least as many people as arrive at the station in that hour. They want the total hire charge to be as low as possible.
Every passenger will pay the same fare. The organisers want the total of the fares to be at least the total hire charge.
Suggest which type of bus, and how many of these buses, the organisers should hire, and find the lowest fare, in cents, that they can charge.
Justify the decisions you make and show your calculations clearly.
parts.answer: Hire 16 single-deck buses (total hire charge $\$7200$; 15 double-deck buses would cost $\$7350$). Lowest fare: 86 cents.

question.answer: (a) 300 (b) 16 single-deck buses (total hire charge $\$7200$); lowest fare 86 cents
skills: a queue that carries over from one hour to the next, where spare bus capacity in the quiet hours cannot be used later
sizing a bus fleet for the busiest hour from trips per hour x passengers per trip, where rounding up to whole buses reverses which bus type is cheaper
break-even fare from the total (not the peak) number of passengers, rounded up to whole cents so that the fares cover the cost
question.solution:
(a)
The buses leave one at a time at equal intervals, so whenever people are waiting they are taken away at a steady rate: the working uses the hourly carrying capacity of the buses.
A single-deck bus makes $60 \div 20 = 3$ round trips an hour, so it carries at most $3 \times 60 = 180$ people an hour.
10 buses carry at most $10 \times 180 = 1800$ people an hour, the steady rate at which waiting people are taken away. [B1]
From 2 pm to 5 pm, fewer than 1800 people arrive in each hour (450, 1050, 1600), so no queue builds up and no one is waiting at 5 pm. The spare capacity in these hours cannot be used later.
5 pm to 6 pm: $2350 - 1800 = 550$ people are waiting at 6 pm. [M1]
6 pm to 7 pm: $550 + 1550 - 1800 = 300$ people are waiting at 7 pm. [A1]
(Tempting wrong answers: 0 from comparing only the 6 pm to 7 pm arrivals with 1800, or from comparing the totals $7000 < 5 \times 1800$.)

(b)
Decision 1 — the buses.
The number of buses is fixed by the busiest hour, 5 pm to 6 pm: this year $2350 \times 1.2 = 2820$ people arrive in that hour. [M1]
Hourly carrying capacity, as in (a): single-deck: 3 trips an hour, $3 \times 60 = 180$ people per bus per hour. Double-deck: $60 \div 30 = 2$ trips an hour, $2 \times 100 = 200$ people per bus per hour. [M1]
Single-deck: $2820 \div 180 = 15.67$, so 16 buses are needed (15 buses carry only 2700). Double-deck: $2820 \div 200 = 14.1$, so 15 buses are needed (14 buses carry only 2800, 20 too few). [M1]
Hire charge: $16 \times \$450 = \$7200$; $15 \times \$490 = \$7350$.
So the organisers should hire 16 single-deck buses, total hire charge $\$7200$. [A1]
(16 single-deck buses carry 2880 people an hour, which is at least the number arriving in every hour this year: 540, 1260, 1920, 2820, 1860.)
Decision 2 — the fare.
Total number of passengers this year $= 7000 \times 1.2 = 8400$ (assuming everyone expected takes a bus and pays). [M1]
$\$7200 \div 8400 = \$0.857\ldots$ [M1]
A fare of 85 cents gives $8400 \times \$0.85 = \$7140 < \$7200$, which does not cover the hire charge; a fare of 86 cents gives $8400 \times \$0.86 = \$7224 \ge \$7200$.
Lowest fare = 86 cents. [A1]
(Tempting wrong routes: 14 double-deck buses at $\$6860$ (rounding 14.1 down); averaging $8400 \div 5 = 1680$ an hour, giving 10 single-deck buses at $\$4500$ or 9 double-deck buses at $\$4410$; leaving out the $20\%$ increase; or dividing by 60 or 100 passengers without the trips per hour. Each of these picks the double-deck bus. If the double-deck buses were hired, the fare would be $\$7350 \div 8400$, giving 88 cents.)
question.syllabus_check: 4052 only: rate (people carried per hour = passengers per trip x round trips per hour, compared with an arrival rate), percentage increase, rounding up to whole buses and whole cents in context, money; problems in real-world contexts — reading an information sheet and making and justifying two decisions. No off-syllabus content (no queueing theory beyond comparing hourly totals; no mixed-fleet optimisation, which the one-type rule excludes).
question.originality_note: New situation: shuttle buses from an MRT station to a festival, planned from last year's hourly arrivals. No real GCE question (corpus searched for bus, shuttle, festival, passengers) and no earlier Set question uses it. Set 1 P2 Q9 chose the smallest water tank that holds enough and fits a base (capacity + fit); this question sizes a fleet against the busiest hour, where the whole-bus step flips the cheaper type, and sets a break-even fare from the total — a different decision on a different object. It is not a price-plan comparison (Set 2 P1 Q15): each bus has one flat hire charge. It differs from Set 2 P1 Q18 (replacement rate = total / lifetime) and P1 Q26 (pipe flow rate): here an hourly carrying capacity is compared with hourly arrivals and a queue is carried across hours. Structure [3, 7] differs from Set 1 P2 Q9 [2, 2, 6] and from GCE 2024/2025 P2 Q9.

answers.(b): Hire 16 single-deck buses (capacity 16 x 60 x 3 = 2880 per hour >= busiest hour 2350 x 1.2 = 2820; cost $7200, cheaper than 15 double-deck at $7350). Total passengers 7000 x 1.2 = 8400; fare >= 7200/8400 = 85.7 cents, so lowest fare = 86 cents

issues: (a) assumes the per-hour capacity model (10 buses x 3 trips x 60 = 1800 per hour; queue 0 until 5-6 pm, 550 at 6 pm, 550 + 1550 - 1800 = 300 at 7 pm). If departures are modelled as discrete simultaneous 20-minute departures from 2 pm, the count at 7 pm depends on whether a 7:00 departure has left, so the answer is model-dependent; the intended reading is clearly the hourly-capacity one.

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both give 300. My check: a single-deck bus makes 3 round trips an hour, so 10 buses carry at most 1800 an hour. Fewer than 1800 arrive in each of 2-3, 3-4 and 4-5 pm, so the queue is 0 at 5 pm and the spare capacity is lost. The queue is 2350 - 1800 = 550 at 6 pm and 550 + 1550 - 1800 = 300 at 7 pm. The blind examiner's reading issue is real. The literal reading of 'the buses run continuously, starting at 2 pm' is that all 10 buses leave together at 2:00, 2:20, ..., 7:00, taking up to 600 people each time. Simulated with exact fractions, that model gives 550 just after the 6:00 departure and, at 7 pm, 900 waiting just before the 7:00 departure and 300 just after it. With staggered buses (one every 2 minutes), it gives 360 just before and 300 just after. The intended answer, 300, therefore survives every model if it is read as 'just after the 7 pm bus has left'. But the stem does not fix the model, and a SEAB stem would. See fixes. Tempting wrong answer: 0, from the totals (7000 < 5 x 1800) or from comparing only the 6-7 pm arrivals with 1800.

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Both give 16 single-deck buses and 86 cents. My check: the busiest hour this year is 2350 x 1.2 = 2820. Single-deck carries 180 a bus an hour: 2820/180 = 15.67, so 16 buses at $7200. Double-deck carries 200 a bus an hour: 2820/200 = 14.1, so 15 buses at $7350. Single-deck is cheaper, although double-deck is cheaper per place ($2.45 against $2.50), so rounding up to whole buses is what reverses the choice. 16 buses carry 2880 an hour, at least every hourly arrival (540, 1260, 1920, 2820, 1860), so no queue forms and all 8400 people ride and pay. Then 7200/8400 = 0.857..., 85 cents gives $7140 < $7200, and 86 cents gives $7224, so the answer is 86 cents. The one-type rule carries weight: without it, a mixed fleet of 9 single-deck and 6 double-deck buses gives exactly 2820 an hour for $6990, so the rule (and its 'regular timetable' reason) must stay.

verdict.key_verdict: The setter and the blind examiner agree on both parts, and my own working confirms 300 people at 7 pm and 16 single-deck buses with a lowest fare of 86 cents. The only open point is the model wording in (a), which the fix below closes without changing the key.
fixes: Fix the carrying model in the stem (the blind examiner's issue). The stem needs one sentence: 'the buses run continuously, starting at 2 pm' reads naturally as all 10 buses leaving together every 20 minutes. Then 7 pm falls on a departure, and the count is 900 just before it and 300 just after. SEAB states the modelling assumption its answer depends on (GCE 2025 P2 Q9(c): 'Erin assumes that each charger charges at a constant maximum rate'). Replace the second bullet with: '• the buses run continuously from 2 pm, leaving the station one at a time at equal intervals, so that whenever people are waiting, the buses take them away from the station at a steady rate,'. This fixes the steady-flow (hourly-capacity) model the key uses, and the answer is unchanged at 300. It does not hand over the idea: the candidate must still build the per-hour capacity (trips x passengers x buses), carry the queue from hour to hour, and see that spare capacity cannot be used later. It also makes (b)'s reason for one bus type ('run to a regular timetable') follow from the stated equal intervals. A minimal alternative, if the bullet is left alone, is to end (a) with '... at 7 pm, just after a bus has left the station.' That gives 300 in every model, but it invites a discrete simulation, so the bullet is the better fix.
verdict.why: All 10 marks are in parts where the candidate decides. In (a) [3], the idea is a queue that carries over, where quiet-hour capacity is lost, with a believable wrong answer of 0. In (b) [7], the item-10 pair of decisions: size each fleet for the busiest hour, where rounding up flips the cheaper type (14 double-deck buses at $6860 and the lower per-place cost both lure candidates to the double-deck bus); then the break-even fare from the total, not the peak, rounded up and justified by 85 cents against 86 cents. The context changes the maths at every step, the numbers are clean (2820, 8400, 6/7 of a dollar), and the wording is SEAB's register. It is at least as demanding as Set 1 P2 Q9 [2, 2, 6] for its marks. It re-skins no GCE 2024/25 question and repeats no earlier Set: Set 2 P1 Q4's bus interchange tests an LCM, and Set 2 P1 Q15 compares price plans by inequalities. It shares no skill with Q2's work rate or Q8's belt speed. It scores 4, not 5, only because the carrying model needs the one-sentence fix. All gates passed.
verdict.session_note: 23 Sep: polish: the one fix — the second assumption bullet now says the buses leave one at a time at equal intervals and take waiting people away at a steady rate (the hourly-capacity model the key uses). Answers unchanged: 300; 16 single-deck, $7200; 86 cents.
